title: Run it as a project, not as four private chats
desc: The Projects group in the sidebar and the eight tabs behind it: three roles, a shared memory pool, and what sharing a conversation does to its encryption.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can create a project, invite a colleague as Editor or Viewer, share a conversation into it knowing exactly what that changes, and tell the project's memory pool apart from your own.

steps.title: Four people, four private chats, one job
steps.bodyMd:
Marieke is projectleider at **Van Dijk Groep**, the sixty-person installation firm near Zwolle. She is preparing a tender for a housing renovation with three colleagues, and right now the job lives in four separate heads: Bas has the supplier prices in his chat history, Karin has the drawings in a notebook only she can open, and Marieke keeps re-pasting the same house style into every prompt.

Nothing there is broken. It is just that a conversation in Bee Flow belongs to one person by default, and so does almost everything else.

A **project** is the exception. It is a named workspace that several colleagues open on the same footing: the conversations they choose to share, the knowledge bases the answers should draw on, the items they built, and a set of standing instructions that every chat inside it obeys. Projects are part of the Enterprise edition, so the row only appears if your organisation has it.

steps.title: The part of the sidebar you have scrolled past
steps.body: This is the top of the sidebar. Once you have a project, a group headed Projects sits lower down: a plus titled New Project beside the heading, a row per project — a colleague's tagged shared — and All projects for the full list. Until then it is one New Project row. The group is hidden in Simple Mode. The list page adds search, sorting and the filters All, Mine and Shared with me.

steps.title: Eight tabs, and each one owns a question
steps.bodyMd:
Open a project and you get one strip of tabs:

- **General** — a description, **Custom Instructions**, the **Extract Project Memories** checkbox, and the colour and icon; the name sits in the header above the tabs.
- **Chats** — the conversations members have shared into the project.
- **Content** — headed *In this project*: notebooks, apps, routines, webpages, tables, agents, knowledge bases and approvals.
- **Knowledge** — the knowledge bases every chat in this project searches. There is a **Create KB** button, and a cap on how many bases one project may carry.
- **Members** — who is in, and at what role.
- **Activity** — what has happened here.
- **Memory** — the project's own memory pool.
- **Danger** — deleting the project. This tab is not hidden from you out of politeness: it is only rendered for the owner.

Custom Instructions are the quiet workhorse. Whatever you type there is added to the system prompt of **every** chat in this project, so the house style gets written once instead of pasted four times a day.

steps.title: Send each request to its tab
steps.instruction: Six things the tender team needs. Match each to the tab that owns it — General, Chats, Content, Knowledge, Members, Activity, Memory or Danger.

pairs.left: "Bas should be able to open the two conversations we are working from."
pairs.note: Chats lists the conversations members have shared. Until someone shares one it reads: No shared conversations yet. Share one to work on it together.

pairs.left: "Answers here should quote our own tender documents, not the open web."
pairs.note: Knowledge holds the bases every chat in this project searches, with a Create KB button for editors.

pairs.left: "The routine Bas built should be reachable by the whole team, not just him."
pairs.note: Content is the In this project list: notebooks, apps, routines, webpages, tables, agents, knowledge bases and approvals. Bas files his routine in himself with Add existing — you can only file in items you own.

pairs.left: "Karin wants to know who changed her role last week."
pairs.note: Activity is the log of the project: who invited whom and at which role, who changed someone's role from which rung to which, who left, whose instructions changed, and which conversations and knowledge bases went in or out.

pairs.left: "Bas keeps re-telling the AI that our standard delivery period is six weeks. It should just know by now."
pairs.note: A fact the team keeps repeating belongs in the project's memory pool, where every member sees it and it is recalled for all of them. A rule about how answers should be written belongs in Custom Instructions on General.

pairs.left: "The tender is lost; Marieke wants the workspace gone."
pairs.note: Danger holds Delete Project, and it only renders for the owner.

steps.title: Owner, Editor, Viewer — and who may hand out which
steps.bodyMd:
On **Members** the owner gets an **Invite Member** panel: pick a user or a group, then a permission. The dropdown offers exactly two, **Viewer** and **Editor**, and the panel says what separates them: *"Editors can update project settings and KBs. Viewers can read and chat in the project."*

**Owner** is not on that list. It is whoever created the project, and it is the only role that can invite, change someone's role, remove a member, or see the Danger tab. The role dropdown beside each member is disabled for everyone else — a member can only remove themselves, which Activity records as leaving rather than as being removed.

A **Viewer** is genuinely read-only. They can open the shared conversations and chat in the project, but they get no Add, Edit or Delete controls — not on Knowledge, not on Content, and not in project memory. The buttons are hidden rather than shown and refused, because the server would refuse them anyway.

steps.question: Marieke wants Bas to add a knowledge base and adjust the project's Custom Instructions, but she does not want him inviting the rest of the office. Which role does she pick when she invites him?

choices.label: Viewer
choices.feedback: A Viewer can read the project and chat in it, but gets no Add, Edit or Delete controls anywhere — including the Knowledge tab and project memory.

choices.label: Owner
choices.feedback: Owner is not on offer in the Invite panel at all: the permission dropdown holds Viewer and Editor only. The owner is whoever created the project, and that role also unlocks Danger.

choices.label: Editor, and she also ticks Extract Project Memories so he can write to the pool
choices.feedback: Two unrelated things. Extract Project Memories decides whether conversations are mined for memories automatically; writing to the pool by hand is already an Editor's right without it.

steps.explanation: Editor is the working role: update project settings and knowledge bases, write project memory, reply in shared conversations. Inviting people, changing roles and deleting the project stay with the owner.

steps.title: Sharing a conversation changes its lock
steps.bodyMd:
It takes two moves, and they are deliberately not one. In the sidebar's ⋯ menu beside a conversation, the projects are listed: click one and the chat is **filed** there. Only then does a second item appear, **Share with project** — and that is the one that publishes it.

A shared conversation lands on the project's **Chats** tab for everyone, under the hint editors get: *"Everyone in this project can read these. Editors can reply."* A thread someone else shared carries their name beside the title, and shows *answering…* while their turn is running.

The warning the app gives you is worth reading twice: *"Shared conversations are encrypted with an organisation key so every project member and background jobs can read them. Your private conversations are unchanged."*

That is literal. A private conversation is sealed with its owner's key; sharing rewrites the messages on the spot under the project's own key, which the organisation holds, because colleagues and background jobs all have to open them. **Stop sharing** re-keys them back.

Both moves are the owner's alone — *"Only a conversation's owner can share it."* Re-encrypting has to read the existing messages first, and on the zero-knowledge tier the key for that exists only while the owner is signed in.

steps.question: Marieke shares her supplier thread into the tender project. What actually happens to that conversation?

choices.label: Its messages are re-encrypted at that moment under the project's own key, which the organisation holds, so members and background jobs can read them — and Stop sharing re-keys them back to her.
Nothing changes about the encryption; the project simply links to the conversation.
choices.feedback: It cannot stay as it was. A private conversation is sealed with its owner's key, which nobody else and no background job holds — sharing has to re-key it or no member could open it.

choices.label: A copy is placed in the project and the original stays private.
choices.feedback: There is no copy. It is the same conversation, now readable by the project — which is why Stop sharing puts it back rather than deleting a duplicate.

choices.label: It stays unreadable to anyone but Editors until Marieke grants a key.
choices.feedback: There is no per-member key handout. Everyone in the project can read a shared conversation; the Editor rung decides who may reply, not who may read.

steps.explanation: Sharing is a re-key, not a link. It is the one place where a conversation stops being sealed to you alone — so decide before you share, and remember that only its owner can share it or take it back.

steps.title: A third memory pool, with names on the cards
steps.bodyMd:
You already have a personal memory. A project adds a second, separate pool, opened from the **Memory** tab, where the panel title reads **Project Memory** and every card shows *by* whoever put it there. The types on offer here are **Instruction, Project, Fact** and **Context**.

Two things to set straight before the team leans on it:

- It is **shared, not private**. Every member sees it and any Editor can delete from it. A Viewer sees the pool with the note *"You have view-only access to this project, so project memory is read-only."*
- It is **empty until you ask for it**. The **Extract Project Memories** checkbox on **General** — *"Automatically learn and recall facts from conversations within this project."* — is off by default. Until it is ticked, nothing is learned here automatically; you can still add entries by hand.

Your own memory is not shut out: inside a project, up to fifteen of your global Instructions and Preferences are merged on top of the project pool. Your other personal memories stay out.

steps.title: Your turn: write the project's Custom Instructions
steps.instruction: Write the Custom Instructions for Marieke's tender project — the text that goes on the General tab and is added to the system prompt of every chat in the project. Three to five sentences. Make them standing rules the assistant should follow every time (language, tone, units, what to always include, what never to do), not a task for today. Keep customer names, addresses and account numbers out of it: this text is read by every chat in the project.
steps.placeholder: e.g. Answer in Dutch unless the question is in English. All prices are ex VAT in euros, and every quotation must name a delivery period. Never promise an installation date without a source in the project's knowledge bases…

steps.title: Three different ways to take something out
steps.bodyMd:
This is where people trip, because three different controls all sound like undo.

- On **Content**, an item you own carries **Remove from project**. That un-files it: it goes back to being standalone and owner-only, untouched, and nothing is deleted. The button is offered narrowly — no viewer sees it, and an editor gets none on a colleague's routine, because only its owner may take it back out. A knowledge base is the loose end: it is linked from the project rather than owned by the item, so any editor may unlink it. **Approvals** are the other extreme — stamped with the project when they are raised and never re-filed, so they list with no remove button at all.
- In the sidebar's ⋯ menu, a filed conversation has two of these. **Stop sharing** takes it off the Chats tab and re-keys it back to its owner, but leaves it filed under the project. **Remove from project** un-files it altogether. Neither deletes the chat — **Delete**, at the bottom of the same menu, does.
- On **Danger**, **Delete Project** ends the workspace: *"Conversations will be unassigned but not deleted. Members and activity history will be removed."* Items on Content are handed back to their owners. The memory pool goes with the project.

steps.question: The tender is lost. Marieke opens Danger and clicks Delete Project. Which outcome should she expect?

choices.label: The shared conversations survive as ordinary chats; members and the activity history are removed, and the project's memory pool goes too.
Everything the team put in the project is deleted with it, conversations included.
choices.feedback: The Danger panel says the opposite before you click: conversations are unassigned, not deleted. Notebooks, routines and the rest are handed back to their owners as standalone items.

choices.label: Nothing happens until every member has left the project first.
choices.feedback: There is no such precondition. Deleting removes the members, which is exactly why the panel warns that membership and activity history are lost.

choices.label: Bas can undo it, because he is an Editor.
choices.feedback: Bas never saw the button: the Danger tab is only rendered for the owner. And there is no undo — the safe move for a finished job is to leave the project alone rather than delete it.

steps.explanation: Deleting a project unpicks the collaboration, not the work. The one thing that genuinely disappears is what only existed because the project existed: its membership, its activity history and its memory pool.

steps.title: Build one — we'll verify it
steps.instruction: In the sidebar, start a new project — the plus beside the Projects heading, or the New Project row if you have none yet — and give it a name (Marieke would use the job name). On the General tab, fill in Custom Instructions with the standing rules you just wrote and save. Then open Members and invite one colleague as Viewer or Editor.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Set a job up as a project.** New Project in the sidebar, then General for the name, Custom Instructions and the colour — and those instructions reach every chat in the project without anyone pasting them.
- **Put people on the right rung.** Owner invites and deletes; Editor updates settings, knowledge and project memory; Viewer reads, chats, and sees the read-only note everywhere else.
- **Share with your eyes open.** Share with project re-keys a conversation to the project so the team and background jobs can read it; Stop sharing re-keys it back, and only its owner can do either.

One habit to take with you: project memory is a team noticeboard, not a private notebook. Put conventions there, keep customer details out of it — and tick Extract Project Memories only when you want the project to start learning on its own.

ex-projects-shared-workspace-instruction.title: Custom Instructions for a shared project
ex-projects-shared-workspace-instruction.task: Write three to five sentences of Custom Instructions for a tender project at Van Dijk Groep — standing rules added to the system prompt of every chat in the project, with no personal or customer data in them.
criteria: Reads as standing rules that apply to every chat in the project (language, tone, units, format, what to always include or never do), not as a one-off task or a question.
At least two concrete, checkable rules rather than vague ambition — for example a language, a currency or VAT convention, a required element in every quotation, or a source requirement.
Fits a shared workspace: written for the whole team, in the second person to the assistant, not as personal preferences about one user.
Contains no customer names, addresses, e-mail addresses, phone numbers or account numbers — nothing that should not be read by every member of the project.
ex-projects-shared-workspace-instruction.guidance: Do not pass a single sentence, a request phrased as a task for today ('write the tender letter'), or text that merely describes the project without instructing the assistant. Do not pass anything containing a real-looking personal detail, even as an example. A learner who writes short, plain, specific rules should pass; polish and length are not the point.

practiceTopic.title: Projects: the shared workspace
practiceTopic.summary: How a project's eight tabs, three roles, shared memory pool and re-keyed conversations fit together for a team working on one job.
facts: A project's tabs are General, Chats, Content, Knowledge, Members, Activity, Memory and Danger; the Danger tab is only rendered for the owner.
Custom Instructions on the General tab are added to the system prompt of every chat in the project; the same tab holds the Extract Project Memories checkbox, which is off by default.
The Invite Member panel offers two permissions, Viewer and Editor: editors can update project settings and KBs, viewers can read and chat in the project. Only the owner invites or changes roles.

Share with project re-encrypts a conversation's messages under the project's key so every member and background jobs can read them; Stop sharing re-keys them back, and only the conversation's owner can do either.
Project memory is a shared pool on the Memory tab with types Instruction, Project, Fact and Context; each card names who added it, and a view-only member is told project memory is read-only.
Inside a project, up to fifteen of your own global Instructions and Preferences are merged on top of the project pool; your other personal memories stay out.

Content lists notebooks, apps, routines, webpages, tables, agents, knowledge bases and approvals under the heading In this project; an owner or editor files in items they own with Add existing and takes them out again with Remove from project, while approvals can never be removed.
Delete Project unassigns the conversations rather than deleting them, but removes the members, the activity history and the project's memory pool.

actionChecks.label: Create a project of your own
actionChecks.hint: Sidebar → New Project, name it, then fill in Custom Instructions on the General tab and save.

endpoints.returns: array of project rows with id, name, description, customInstructions, knowledgeBaseIds, color, icon, ownerId, extractMemories and permission ('owner'/'editor'/'viewer')

criteria.label: A project you own exists
criteria.hint: Click New Project in the sidebar and give it a name — the project you create is yours. The Custom Instructions you type on the General tab are stored inside the project, where this check cannot look.
criteria.rule: GET /api/projects → at least one row whose ownerId is the learner (rows check; shared projects carry someone else’s ownerId)
